title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Sep 25, 2026
intro: This edition leans on two source-measured wins — a harness that trades repeated context for reusable control code, and a codebase knowledge graph — alongside two safety incidents worth auditing your own agent for before they become yours.

cards.title: Turn repeated task-control decisions into reusable code, not repeated context
cards.problem: Agents handling streams of related tasks re-derive the same routing and control decisions inside every task's context, burning tokens and calls on decisions the agent already made before.
cards.apply: Convert recurring control-flow decisions into a failure-guided, growing harness: log execution traces per function, repair the harness code (not the prompt) when a trace fails, and gate updates behind a success-first check so a repair can't roll back a prior fix.
cards.result: In the paper's WebArena-Verified/BrowseComp-Plus tests, this cut LLM calls 76–92% and inference cost 74–99% versus a standard tool-calling agent, while holding 44.7–45.3% success across model sizes where tool-calling collapsed to 6.7% at the 4B scale.

evidence.note: The paper reports call-count, cost, and success-rate deltas from its own WebArena-Verified/BrowseComp-Plus evaluation.

cards.title: Audit turns, cache lifetime, and effort level — not just the token price — to control task cost
cards.problem: The same per-token price produces very different per-task bills, because turn count, cache reads, output-token volume, and effort level each multiply the effective cost independently of the sticker price.
cards.apply: Compact long sessions at natural breaks instead of letting them idle past the cache lifetime, keep effort at Medium unless a task is complex enough to justify High's added thinking tokens, and route lookup subagents to Sonnet/Haiku instead of the main model.
cards.result: Anthropic's own breakdown: cache reads run $0.20/Mtok (60% cheaper than Opus 5), a typical 60K-output-token task costs $1.20, High effort adds ~$0.40 in thinking tokens per task, and a $0.25 compaction saves $0.025 on every turn after it.

evidence.note: Figures are Anthropic's own cost breakdown for Claude Code on Opus 5.5.

cards.title: Set explicit cache breakpoints instead of hoping the prefix matches
cards.problem: Prompt caching often underperforms silently: without control over where the cache boundary falls, a small prompt change anywhere upstream can knock a request out of cache.
cards.apply: Use GPT-6's caching diagnostics to see where requests are missing cache, and place explicit breakpoints so static content (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples) stays ahead of the boundary and variable content stays after it.
cards.result: OpenAI reports the changes raise cache hit rates and lower both latency and cost, though the exact size of the improvement depends on your own prompt shape.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement claims the improvement; no third-party or quantified figure is available to confirm the size of the effect.

cards.title: Give coding agents a codebase knowledge graph instead of flat file search
cards.problem: Coding assistants that treat a repo as a pool of text struggle with multi-file reasoning and deep dependencies, burning context window on token-heavy searches that still miss structural relationships.
cards.apply: Parse the repo into a queryable knowledge graph (Graphify uses tree-sitter AST extraction plus community detection) covering files, symbols, and cross-file call/import edges, expose it to the agent over MCP, and have it traverse the graph for context instead of grepping.
cards.result: Graphify's own benchmarks show a LOCOMO recall@10 of 0.497 (45.3% QA accuracy, 76% on its 50-question subset) and lifted ERPNext key-fact coverage from 70.8% to 82.0% versus flat retrieval — though reviewers note plain grep can still feel faster on mid-sized repos.

evidence.note: Numbers are Graphify's own reported benchmark results.

cards.title: Cap and log any code path that lets your agent harness bundle-upload local files
cards.problem: A coding agent's harness reportedly packaged 42,411 files from one developer's machine and attempted 564 uploads to the vendor's cloud, without the kind of explicit consent a bulk export should require.
cards.apply: Put an explicit allowlist, a size/rate cap, and an audit log on any code path in your agent harness that can bundle and transmit local files — treat 'upload the workspace' as a privileged action, not a background default.
cards.result: As reported, a runaway or unauthorized bulk upload gets blocked and logged locally before it leaves the machine, instead of surfacing only after developers notice their own files leaving without a support ticket.

evidence.note: File and attempt counts are as reported; treat them as an as-reported claim, not an independently verified audit.

cards.title: Strip debug config keys that can flip permissions before you ship an agent client
cards.problem: A single undocumented debug preference key in Meta's Muse desktop client let an unprivileged local process redirect the assistant's voice-dictation traffic and inherit its OS permissions, with no admin prompt required.
cards.apply: Audit every debug/diagnostic config key your agent client ships with in production for whether an unprivileged local process can write it, and strip or lock behind a build-time flag anything that can redirect network endpoints or expand permissions.
cards.result: As reported, Meta's fix — stripping the debug preference from production builds — closes the exact path an attacker used to intercept credentials and audio and inject hidden instructions through the trusted agent.

evidence.note: Based on security researcher Patrick Wardle's disclosure, as reported; Meta treated it as a configuration defect rather than filing a CVE.

cards.title: Wire automated red-teaming into agent CI, not just spot-checks
cards.problem: Agent regressions and adversarial failure modes usually surface in production because testing stays manual and ad hoc between releases.
cards.apply: Add an automated red-teaming and regression-test pass to your agent's CI pipeline so adversarial and edge-case prompts run on every change, following LangSmith Engine's red-teaming plus automated-testing pattern.
cards.result: LangChain claims failure modes get caught before a release ships instead of after users trigger them.

evidence.note: LangChain's own product announcement; no independent measurement of detection rate is available.

cards.title: Score agent memory on cost and latency, not just recall accuracy
cards.problem: Most agent memory benchmarks are conversational QA where the question itself hints at which fact to retrieve, and they report only accuracy — hiding the cost/latency tradeoffs a memory system makes to hit that score.
cards.apply: Evaluate your agent's memory system the way DolphinBench does: task-completion tests built from real usage history rather than QA-shaped prompts, with cost and latency reported alongside accuracy, and tasks that fail without the relevant history to confirm the memory access actually mattered.
cards.result: A memory upgrade that looks better on accuracy alone stops passing silently if it doubles cost or latency to get there.

evidence.note: DolphinBench's abstract describes the benchmark design; it does not publish comparative accuracy/cost numbers to cite.
